name: Copper
mobility: IMMOBILE (deficiency on YOUNGEST leaves & growing points)

overview.whyImportant: Copper is a cofactor of photosynthetic and respiratory enzymes and is critical for lignin (stem strength), pollen viability and grain set. Deficiency is uncommon but occurs on sandy, peaty/organic and heavily-limed soils, causing wilting young shoots, twisted tips and poor grain set.

plantFunctions.roleInsidePlant: Cofactor of oxidase enzymes, plastocyanin (photosynthesis), lignin synthesis.
plantFunctions.photosynthesis: Part of plastocyanin in electron transport.
plantFunctions.vegetativeGrowth: Lignification for firm stems; deficiency causes limp/twisted young growth.
plantFunctions.flowering: Essential for pollen viability and fertilisation.
plantFunctions.yieldContribution: Grain/seed set and stem strength; deficiency causes 'ear-tip sterility' in cereals.

whyDeficiencyHappens.why: Cu availability drops as pH rises.
Usually adequate; leaching in very acid sandy soils.
Organic matter strongly binds Cu, making it unavailable — classic peat-soil Cu deficiency.
Low Cu cycling (but HIGH organic matter also locks Cu).

whyDeficiencyHappens.condition: Nutrient imbalance / excess N, P, Zn, Fe
whyDeficiencyHappens.why: High N dilutes Cu; excess Zn/Fe/P antagonise Cu uptake.
Ignoring Cu on sandy/peaty soils; over-liming.

symptoms.note: Cu IMMOBILE — youngest leaves/tips affected. Signature: wilting/twisting of young shoots, pale tips, poor grain set.
symptoms.early: Youngest leaves pale, tips begin to wilt/curl.
symptoms.middle: Twisted, limp young leaves with withered tips ('pig-tail'), pale colour.
symptoms.severe: Dieback of growing points, white/withered tips, poor flowering, blank ear tips in cereals.
symptoms.youngLeaves: First affected: pale, twisted, curled, tip die-back.
symptoms.fruit: Poor grain/seed set; blank ear tips.
symptoms.wholePlant: Healthy old leaves but wilting twisted young growth and poor grain set — top-down pattern.

cropWiseSymptoms.symptoms: Chlorotic rolled young leaves with withered tips, poor grain set on peaty/sandy soils.
Pale twisted young leaves, poor pod set (rare, sandy/organic soils).
Young-leaf chlorosis, poor pod set on light soils.
Wilting pale young leaves, poor fruit set.
Twisted pale young growth, poor set (rare).
Wilting pale young tips, poor fruit set.
Young leaves pale, tips wither and curl (pig-tail), poor tip grain set.
Pale twisted young leaves on sandy soils, poor grain set.
Pale young leaves, poor pod set (rare).
Young-leaf chlorosis, poor set on light soils.
Chlorotic drooping young leaves with tip die-back on sandy/organic soils.

howToFix.soilApplicationDose: 2-4 kg/acre basal (once every few years; residual)
howToFix.methodOfApplication: Soil basal (residual) or dilute foliar; often coincides with Cu-fungicide sprays
howToFix.precautions: Cu is easily TOXIC — use low doses, add lime to foliar; do not over-apply (builds up in soil).
Low dose; Cu accumulates — avoid repeated heavy use.

methodOfApplication.broadcast: Low-dose CuSO4 basal + incorporate (residual for years).
methodOfApplication.foliarSpray: Dilute 0.2-0.3% CuSO4 + lime; Cu-fungicide sprays (Bordeaux/copper oxychloride) also supply some Cu.
methodOfApplication.seedTreatment: Cu seed treatment used in some cereals on deficient soils.

toxicity.whatHappens: Cu toxicity is a REAL risk — Cu accumulates from repeated CuSO4/copper-fungicide use.
toxicity.plantToxicitySymptoms: Induced iron deficiency (young-leaf chlorosis), stunted brown roots, reduced growth.
toxicity.yieldLoss: Via root damage and induced Fe deficiency.
toxicity.correctionMethods: Stop Cu inputs; apply Fe; lime acid soils to reduce Cu availability; add organic matter to bind Cu.

prevention: Apply Cu only where soil-tested deficient (sandy/peaty soils).
Use low doses — Cu is residual and toxic in excess.
Account for Cu supplied by copper fungicides.
Avoid over-liming (locks Cu) and excess P/Zn (antagonism).
Manage organic soils carefully (they bind Cu).
Foliar Cu for quick correction at low concentration.
commonFarmerMistakes: Applying Cu without a soil test (toxicity risk).
Repeated heavy CuSO4 + copper-fungicide use causing Cu build-up.
Foliar CuSO4 without lime, scorching leaves.
Confusing Cu (twisted wilting tips) with other micro deficiencies.
Over-applying Cu and inducing Fe deficiency.
Assuming Cu deficiency is common (it's not — verify).
Repeated Cu on the same field yearly.
Ignoring organic-matter binding on peat soils.
expertTips: Confirm Cu deficiency by soil test before applying — it's uncommon and toxic in excess.

Use LOW doses; Cu is highly residual.
Count Cu supplied by Bordeaux/copper-oxychloride fungicide sprays.
Add lime to foliar CuSO4 to prevent scorch (Bordeaux principle).
On peaty/organic soils, expect Cu binding — foliar works better.
Avoid over-liming and excess P/Zn (Cu antagonists).
Watch for induced Fe deficiency from Cu excess.

One basal Cu dose lasts several years.
Balance micronutrients — don't stack Cu with heavy Zn/Fe.

New growth responds; old leaves stay normal.
Cu seed treatment on chronically deficient cereal soils.
Never routinely add Cu 'just in case'.
Add organic matter to buffer Cu toxicity on contaminated soils.
Spray in cool hours to reduce scorch.
Don't tank-mix Cu with strongly alkaline foliar (except proper Bordeaux).

Prioritise diagnosis — mis-applied Cu does more harm than good.
